item.title: Valkyries' run of Ballhalla brilliance ends as Dream dominate Game 2 of WNBA Finals
item.description: Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese (5) knocks the ball away from Golden State Valkyries guard Tiffany Hayes (15) during the second half of the WNBA Finals Game 2 at Chase Center in San Francisco, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Carlos Avila Gonzalez/S.F. Chronicle) The Golden State Valkyries suffered their first-ever playoff loss at Chase Center, dropping Game 2 of the WNBA Finals 79-65 to the Atlanta Dream on Monday. The Valkyries' defense typically fuels their offense, but they couldn't disrupt a determined Angel Reese quite enough to generate any meaningful runs. Head coach Natalie Nakase tapped 11 players off the bench to throw Atlanta's way, but not one could get offensive momentum going. Reese took over to the tune of 30 points and 16 rebounds, the third time a player has ever totaled at least 30 and 15 in a WNBA Finals game. Gabby Williams , meanwhile, wasn't able to carry the load for Golden State as she has throughout the playoffs. She was inefficient, shooting 3-of-15 from the field for 14 points with two rebounds. The Valkyries shot close to 20% from 3 and on the lower end of 30% from the field - similar to their output in Game 1, which they won by a nose with stifling defense down the stretch. The Valkyries scored nine points in the third quarter to the Dream's 21. The Dream went on an 11-0 run in the fourth quarter to take a commanding 21-point lead midway through and Golden State's offense turned frantic as a result. The Valkyries succumbed to the Dream's defensive pressure and committed 19 turnovers, resulting in 24 points. The sloppiness translated into fouls, as the Valkyries sent Atlanta to the line 31 times while getting to the line 17 times despite Rhyne Howard and Reese landing in foul trouble. After regretting her lack of aggression in the second half of Game 1, Reese took control instantly on Monday with forceful attacks at the rim. She didn't hold back. Early in the first quarter broadcast cameras caught her and Aminata Gueye exchanging heated words at the foul line. In the second quarter, she trucked through Laeticia Amihere driving to the rim for a layup. It was the Valkyries' fourth loss of more than 10 points this season. Golden State will try to take the lead again on Wednesday in Atlanta for Game 3. Subscribe There’s more to San Francisco with the Chronicle. Subscribe today for just 25¢. This article originally published at Valkyries' run of Ballhalla brilliance ends as Dream dominate Game 2 of WNBA Finals .

item.title: Brewers-Rays World Series inspires both dreams and nightmares around MLB
item.description: It’s a dream World Series matchup for the Major League Baseball Players Association, which has been shouting to the world that baseball’s competitive balance is just fine, and there is absolutely no reason to dramatically change the economic system. It’s a nightmare World Series matchup for Major League Baseball , which has stressed to everyone who’d listen that that a salary cap is desperately needed, even running advertisements into the the postseason. It’s a dream World Series matchup for the fans of two small-market franchises whose shrewd front offices continually outsmart their big-spending brethren. It a nightmare World Series matchup for the TV executives with two small-markets – including one which failed to even sell out several games of the postseason – that could lead to the lowest ratings in World Series history. It’s a dream World Series matchup if you love the underdog, and learn about players you’ve never heard of in your life. It’s a nightmare if you love star power, with only one MVP, one presumptive Cy Young winner and not a single veteran with a ticket into Cooperstown. Either way, it’s the Tampa Bays and the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series. This is the first World Series between two small-market franchises since the Florida Marlins and Cleveland in 1997. And it’s the first time in 35 years that two World Series teams ranked among the bottom half of spending when the Minnesota Twins (15 th out of 26 teams) and Atlanta (19 th ) met in the 1991 World Series. The Brewers have baseball’s 19 th -lowest payroll and the Rays have the 25 th -lowest. No matter who wins, we will have the first small-market World Series champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals. While Bruce Meyer, executive director of the players union will be vehemently arguing to the assembled media that there’s no reason for a salary cap (“Don’t believe what you hear from the owner who’s complaining") and commissioner Rob Manfred and MLB executives will be laying out reasons why a cap is essential for baseball’s future (“It defies human experience to ask a fan to think that the bottom end of that gap has the same opportunity to win as the top") two plucky small-market franchises will be fighting on the field for the first World Series championship in their franchise history. The Brewers, who haven’t been to the World Series in 44 years, and the Rays, who have twice been to the World Series since 2008 but came up empty, are two of baseball’s last five franchises who have never won a title – joining the San Diego Padres, Seattle Mariners and Colorado Rockies. Once we get past the rhetoric whether this matchup is great or god-awful for baseball, we’ve got two teams who have proven all year that they are the best teams in baseball and belong on the big stage. The Brewers won a franchise-record and MLB-leading 103 games, winning the NL Central in a runaway and cruising though the playoffs, sweeping the two-time World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS.
item.content:encoded: It’s a dream World Series matchup for the Major League Baseball Players Association, which has been shouting to the world that baseball’s competitive balance is just fine, and there is absolutely no reason to dramatically change the economic system. It’s a nightmare World Series matchup for Major League Baseball , which has stressed to everyone who’d listen that that a salary cap is desperately needed, even running advertisements into the the postseason. It’s a dream World Series matchup for the fans of two small-market franchises whose shrewd front offices continually outsmart their big-spending brethren. It a nightmare World Series matchup for the TV executives with two small-markets – including one which failed to even sell out several games of the postseason – that could lead to the lowest ratings in World Series history. It’s a dream World Series matchup if you love the underdog, and learn about players you’ve never heard of in your life. It’s a nightmare if you love star power, with only one MVP, one presumptive Cy Young winner and not a single veteran with a ticket into Cooperstown. Either way, it’s the Tampa Bays and the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series. This is the first World Series between two small-market franchises since the Florida Marlins and Cleveland in 1997. And it’s the first time in 35 years that two World Series teams ranked among the bottom half of spending when the Minnesota Twins (15 th out of 26 teams) and Atlanta (19 th ) met in the 1991 World Series. The Brewers have baseball’s 19 th -lowest payroll and the Rays have the 25 th -lowest. No matter who wins, we will have the first small-market World Series champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals. While Bruce Meyer, executive director of the players union will be vehemently arguing to the assembled media that there’s no reason for a salary cap (“Don’t believe what you hear from the owner who’s complaining") and commissioner Rob Manfred and MLB executives will be laying out reasons why a cap is essential for baseball’s future (“It defies human experience to ask a fan to think that the bottom end of that gap has the same opportunity to win as the top") two plucky small-market franchises will be fighting on the field for the first World Series championship in their franchise history. The Brewers, who haven’t been to the World Series in 44 years, and the Rays, who have twice been to the World Series since 2008 but came up empty, are two of baseball’s last five franchises who have never won a title – joining the San Diego Padres, Seattle Mariners and Colorado Rockies. Once we get past the rhetoric whether this matchup is great or god-awful for baseball, we’ve got two teams who have proven all year that they are the best teams in baseball and belong on the big stage. The Brewers won a franchise-record and MLB-leading 103 games, winning the NL Central in a runaway and cruising though the playoffs, sweeping the two-time World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS. The Rays won an American-League leading 98 games, capturing the powerful AL East, and survived a grueling six-game series against the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS. Next stop, saving the grand ol’ game of baseball, with these two teams showing that you don’t need $700 million players. They are the antithesis to the three-outcome brand we’ve become accustomed over over the years. These two teams, who met the first weekend of the season with the Brewers winning two of the three games at American Family Field, are actually mirror images of one another. Their offenses put relentless pressure on you. They don’t strike out. They put the ball in play. They run. They hit-and-run. They bunt. They steal bases. They have speed. They play exceptional defense. This will be only the second World Series since 1918 that each team stole at least 162 bases during the season, with the Brewers the first World Series team since the 2014 Royals to have more stolen bases than home runs. Then, there are intriguing similarities: The Brewers have The Miz (Jacob Misiorowski). The Rays have The Raz (Drew Ramussen). The Brewers have 22-year-old Jackson Chourio. The Rays have 23-year-old superstar Junior Caminero. The Brewers have beloved captain and team leader Christian Yelich. The Rays have beloved unofficial captain and team leader Yandy Diaz. The Brewers have speedster David Hamilton. The Rays have Chandler Simpson, perhaps the game’s fastest player. The Brewers have a powerful bullpen led by closer Trevor Megill. The Rays have a powerful bullpen led by closer Bryan Baker.cThe Brewers have NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, a former Ray. The Rays have ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta, a former Brewer. The Brewers have one of the shortest teams in baseball with three primary players who are 5-foot-10 or shorter: (Luis Lara (5-7), Sal Frelick (5-9) and Williams Contreras (5-10). The Rays have one of the shortest teams with three players who are 5-foot-9 or shorter: Cedric Mullins (5-7), Richie Palacios (5-8) and Taylor Walls (5-9). The Brewers don’t have a single everyday player who was signed as a free agent. The Rays don’t have a single everyday player who was signed as a free agent. The Brewers badly wanted two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline, only to be out-bid by the Dodgers. The Rays badly wanted Skubal at the trade deadline and were outbid too. The Brewers acquired their MVP, Christian Yelich, in a trade. The Brewers acquired their MVP candidate Junior Caminero, in a trade. Milwaukee prides itself on bratwurst. Tampa Bay prides itself on Cuban sandwiches. Two brilliant organizations, each finding the edge through analytics and scouting, with the Rays having more pro scouts than any team in baseball, going head-to-head in what looms as a riveting matchup. This World Series should be an absolute doozy. No matter who bothers to watch. Follow Nightengale on X: @Bnightengale This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Brewers-Rays World Series inspires both dreams and nightmares around MLB

item.title: Inside Shakur Stevenson's shocking Zuffa exit — and why it exposes the limits of Dana White's control in boxing
item.description: "In boxing, you can never have control. It's out of control. But you've got to be up for being in that world." That was Eddie Hearn's warning when TKO — the parent company of UFC and WWE — entered the sport with Zuffa Boxing earlier this year. A little over three months with Shakur Stevenson has given Dana White a taste of exactly what his promotional rival meant. On Monday, Stevenson announced he had secured his release from White's promotion , ending a partnership that produced multiple rounds of failed negotiations and not a single fight. Stevenson, the WBO super lightweight world champion and Uncrowned's No. 4 pound-for-pound fighter , was Zuffa's most high-profile signing since its inception in January. His departure exposes a fundamental problem with importing the UFC model into boxing: Signing a star does not give you control over the fights that make him valuable. With UFC, TKO operates from a position of overwhelming strength. It controls most of the opponents its fighters want to face, and the platform on which these fights can happen. A fighter can push for a different opponent or a better offer, but the UFC ultimately controls whether those alternatives materialize. The choice is largely to accept the company's terms or wait, as UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland recently discovered . With Stevenson, the balance of power was different. Although Zuffa had secured his signature, all of his most desirable opponents were outside its stable. Their purses, schedules, and willingness to fight him — and vice versa — were beyond White's control. Shakur Stevenson's (third from right) time with Dana White's Zuffa Boxing ended Monday without a single fight. Ed Mulholland via Getty Images The obvious starting point for the four-division champion was Jose "Rayo" Valenzuela, the most high-profile lightweight in Zuffa's stable. Stevenson instantly dismissed that matchup. White, who had said he wouldn't work with other promoters, was forced to look beyond his own roster almost immediately. There, he encountered the same obstacles that have frustrated boxing's established promoters for decades. A unification fight with WBA super lightweight champion Gary Antuanne Russell was explored, but Russell wanted $3 million — a number Zuffa was not willing to pay. A mandatory defense against Raymond Muratalla proved similarly unfeasible. There were attempts to place Stevenson on the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua undercard, potentially against Manny Pacquiao, but those discussions soon hit a financial roadblock. With nothing else on the table, Zuffa then pivoted and let Stevenson try to make a fight with WBO welterweight champion Devin Haney. A matchup between Stevenson and Haney — two of boxing's leading stars under 30 — had been explored earlier this year while Haney was considering signing with Zuffa. item.dc:creator: Darshan Desai
item.content:encoded: "In boxing, you can never have control. It's out of control. But you've got to be up for being in that world." That was Eddie Hearn's warning when TKO — the parent company of UFC and WWE — entered the sport with Zuffa Boxing earlier this year. A little over three months with Shakur Stevenson has given Dana White a taste of exactly what his promotional rival meant. On Monday, Stevenson announced he had secured his release from White's promotion , ending a partnership that produced multiple rounds of failed negotiations and not a single fight. Stevenson, the WBO super lightweight world champion and Uncrowned's No. 4 pound-for-pound fighter , was Zuffa's most high-profile signing since its inception in January. His departure exposes a fundamental problem with importing the UFC model into boxing: Signing a star does not give you control over the fights that make him valuable. With UFC, TKO operates from a position of overwhelming strength. It controls most of the opponents its fighters want to face, and the platform on which these fights can happen. A fighter can push for a different opponent or a better offer, but the UFC ultimately controls whether those alternatives materialize. The choice is largely to accept the company's terms or wait, as UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland recently discovered . With Stevenson, the balance of power was different. Although Zuffa had secured his signature, all of his most desirable opponents were outside its stable. Their purses, schedules, and willingness to fight him — and vice versa — were beyond White's control. Shakur Stevenson's (third from right) time with Dana White's Zuffa Boxing ended Monday without a single fight. Ed Mulholland via Getty Images The obvious starting point for the four-division champion was Jose "Rayo" Valenzuela, the most high-profile lightweight in Zuffa's stable. Stevenson instantly dismissed that matchup. White, who had said he wouldn't work with other promoters, was forced to look beyond his own roster almost immediately. There, he encountered the same obstacles that have frustrated boxing's established promoters for decades. A unification fight with WBA super lightweight champion Gary Antuanne Russell was explored, but Russell wanted $3 million — a number Zuffa was not willing to pay. A mandatory defense against Raymond Muratalla proved similarly unfeasible. There were attempts to place Stevenson on the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua undercard, potentially against Manny Pacquiao, but those discussions soon hit a financial roadblock. With nothing else on the table, Zuffa then pivoted and let Stevenson try to make a fight with WBO welterweight champion Devin Haney. A matchup between Stevenson and Haney — two of boxing's leading stars under 30 — had been explored earlier this year while Haney was considering signing with Zuffa. When Haney joined DAZN , though, it was thought to be out of the picture because the boxers were aligned with different networks. However, with Zuffa and Paramount unable to make a meaningful fight for Stevenson themselves, they were prepared to let him fight on DAZN. Zuffa waved the white flag, so to speak — White and company had to agree to let their biggest star make his promotional debut … on a rival broadcaster. But that didn't help much. Disagreements over money and weight proved decisive, and in the end, Zuffa was left with no Stevenson-Haney fight, no opponent to match Stevenson with on its own show, and no clear next step. Stevenson wanted around $15 million to face Haney, sources close to the situation told Uncrowned. According to boxing reporter Sean Zittel, he sought the same number to take on Valenzuela under the Zuffa banner, while the promotion offered $7 million. Stevenson's team told Uncrowned's Ariel Helwani on Monday that he had been “frustrated as of late" with the direction of his career under Zuffa. Conor Benn infamously made $15 million for his Zuffa debut against Regis Prograis. The industry consensus was that Zuffa deliberately overpaid to make the offer unmatchable for Hearn’s Matchroom before moving forward with a deal closer to market value. But that strategy also created a benchmark. And Stevenson felt he could demand that sum too. Stevenson exercised the bargaining power that comes with being a star in boxing. He rejected an opponent, refused to fight at welterweight, and demanded top dollar for matchups. That is the difficulty facing Zuffa. The names it wants to attract are already stars in their own rights. They have options. Zuffa has to navigate fighters' choices and freedom — and worse, most of the opponents they need to fight to make these deals work exist largely outside its control. Zuffa has been linked to Ryan Garcia, who has two fights remaining on his DAZN contract. But with Teofimo Lopez, Haney and Stevenson outside its roster, signing Garcia would present a familiar problem: Securing the star while leaving his biggest fights dependent on deals with rival promoters and broadcasters. What can Zuffa deliver for Garcia that it couldn't for Stevenson? Stevenson, meanwhile, is now a free agent. And there is an obvious choice for his next move. Garcia, Haney, Russell, Muratalla, Dalton Smith, Floyd Schofield and others — nearly all of the potential Stevenson opponents — have one thing in common: They fight on DAZN. Stevenson's next move must put him in the DAZN sphere, whether that is through a promotional agreement with Matchroom, PBC, Top Rank, or Golden Boy, or a direct deal with DAZN, following in the footsteps of Haney and Lopez. Shakur Stevenson hasn't fought since a January win over Teofimo Lopez. Ed Mulholland via Getty Images Announcing his free agent status, the WBO super lightweight champion said: "This time, I want to tell the fans and tell everyone in the public that I'm now taking my career in my own hands, and I'm starting my own promotional company, and I'm willing to work with other promoters and anybody else that's out there that's willing to be serious about my career as I am about my career." With Stevenson looking to start his own promotional entity, a direct deal with DAZN may be the way to go. Stevenson can arrange his own fights with a budget from the streaming service and pay a promoter to be the service provider for the card, handle logistics, undercard bouts, and put together the event. Stevenson was offered a deal directly by DAZN in the summer, which he described as "very similar" to his Zuffa offer. But here is the issue Stevenson will likely face: When DAZN made him that proposal, it was competing with a rival attempting to lock down all of the top talent in the sport. Now that DAZN has Lopez, Haney, and Garcia on its platform, and Zuffa is no longer in the picture for Stevenson, the leverage is tilted more in DAZN's favor. Essentially, yesterday's price is not today's price, and Stevenson may not get the same money he was being offered earlier this year. Because if he doesn't sign with DAZN or a promoter on the network, where else can he even go? A move to DAZN would put Stevenson on the same platform as many of the opponents he wants. It would not, however, resolve the disagreements over money and weight that helped derail the Haney fight. Stevenson has taken back control of his career. Now, he needs to show a willingness to compromise to make the best fights.

item.title: Jaxon Smith-Njigba is dominating the NFL receiving race
item.description: There is one receiver in the NFL who is in a league of his own. Jaxon Smith-Njigba of the Seattle Seahawks has opened a huge lead in total receiving yards through six weeks. Smith-Njigba has 717 yards on 49 catches, seven of which have gone for touchdowns. He leads Chris Olave of the New Orleans Saints by 137 yards. Olave is three yards better than CeeDee Lamb of the Dallas Cowboys. A look at the top 10 in receiving yards after six weeks. t-10. Tetairoa McMillan, Carolina Panthers Receiving yards: 471 t-10. item.title: Fantasy Football Week 7 Injury Report: Jalen Hurts, Mike Evans, Davante Adams And More
item.description: London, United Kingdom - October 11: Jalen Hurts of Philadelphia Eagles in action during the NFL match between Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 11, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images) DeFodi Images via Getty Images We’ve nearly reached the halfway point of the 2026 fantasy football regular season. If you still have a relatively healthy squad, you’re one of the lucky ones. Week 6 yet again featured a number of big-name players going down with injuries, including a few that have long-term ramifications. With the Buffalo Bills, Jacksonville Jaguars, Los Angeles Chargers and Washington Commanders headed into a bye in Week 7, fantasy managers may be scrambling for replacements up and down their rosters. Every week, we’ll be breaking down the biggest injury news that could shape your fantasy football lineup moving forward. Let’s dive into all of the most notable updates ahead of Week 7. Notable QB Injuries Eagles QB Jalen Hurts (blood clot) When Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts popped up on the injury report with a calf injury leading into Week 5, it raised some alarms. However, Hurts played through the injury and practiced fully last Wednesday, which seemed to suggest it wasn’t a big deal. About that. On Thursday, the Eagles announced that Hurts had been diagnosed with a superficial blood clot and would miss their Week 6 game against the Carolina Panthers. Two days later, they placed Hurts on injured reserve , which guaranteed that he would be out through Week 10. On Monday, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Hurts is now expected to miss the rest of the season “after doctors discovered multiple blood clots” in his lungs. He’ll be on blood thinners for at least the next three months, which means he’s not allowed to participate in football activities during that span. Tanner McKee stepped in for Hurts on Sunday and went 26-of-45 for 215 yards, one touchdown and zero interceptions. He was able to keep DeVonta Smith (seven catches for 75 yards and a touchdown) and Dallas Goedert (six catches for 61 yards) afloat, so all hope is not lost for the Eagles’ skill-position players. If anything, the Eagles might be in more trailing, pass-friendly game scripts moving forward. Notable RB Injuries Commanders RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) Washington Commanders running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt originally hurt his groin in training camp and missed the team’s final two preseason games, but he was able to play through it once the regular season started. However, he aggravated the injury in the Commanders’ Week 5 tie against the New York Giants and missed their Week 6 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. It went from bad to worse on Monday, as the Commanders placed him on IR , which means he’ll now miss at least their next four games. If anything, the Eagles might be in more trailing, pass-friendly game scripts moving forward. Notable RB Injuries Commanders RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt (groin) Washington Commanders running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt originally hurt his groin in training camp and missed the team’s final two preseason games, but he was able to play through it once the regular season started. However, he aggravated the injury in the Commanders’ Week 5 tie against the New York Giants and missed their Week 6 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. It went from bad to worse on Monday, as the Commanders placed him on IR , which means he’ll now miss at least their next four games. Rachaad White took over as their lead running back against the Niners, although the Commanders fell into an early deficit and never got their ground game on track. White is worth a pickup if he’s available on your league’s waiver wire, but it’s hard to have much faith in him in standard 10-team leagues. He’ll be a desperation flex option in 12-team leagues or deeper, though, particularly in points-per-reception formats. Browns RB Quinshon Judkins (ankle) Cleveland Browns running back Quinshon Judkins suffered a “tweak” in his ankle during their Week 5 loss to the New York Jets, according to head coach Todd Monken. He wound up missing practice Wednesday and Thursday and got in a limited practice Friday, which earned him a questionable tag heading into their Week 6 game against the division-rival Baltimore Ravens. But after testing out his ankle in pregame warmups, he got ruled out. With Judkins sidelined, Jaleel McLaughlin and Audric Estime split carries for the Browns. McLaughlin had nine carries for a team-high 41 yards, while Estime had nine carries for 19 yards. Quarterback Deshaun Watson also chipped in with eight carries for 29 yards. If Judkins can’t return in Week 7, Dylan Sampson could further muddy the Browns’ backfield. He’s been on injured reserve since suffering a knee injury in the season opener, but he got in two limited practices last week. He’s worth picking up given Judkins’ uncertain status, particularly in PPR leagues. Cardinals RB Jeremiyah Love (ankle) Arizona Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love has been dealing with ankle injuries ever since the preseason. According to Darren Urban of the team’s website , he aggravated a left ankle injury “a couple of times” against the New York Giants in Week 4, and trying to play through it hasn’t helped. “We felt like it wasn’t improving and maybe even getting a little bit worse,” Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters Friday . “At that point, it’s like, if it’s not improving, it’s getting a little bit worse, we got to do what’s right for the player.” Bam Knight had 15 carries for a team-high 80 yards in the Cardinals’ upset win over the Los Angeles Rams, while Tyler Allgeier had 18 carries for 38 yards. If the Cardinals decide to rest Love again in Week 7, the more explosive Knight appears to be the preferred play over Allgeier. Notable WR Injuries 49ers WR Mike Evans (Achilles) San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans came into Week 6 nursing both ribs and Achilles injuries, which had him questionable heading into Monday Night Football . That wasn’t apparent early on against the Commanders, as he erupted with three catches for 94 yards in the first half. However, Evans aggravated his injury after hauling in a 16-yard pass shortly before halftime. He was questionable to return at first, but the Niners ruled him out early in the third quarter, according to ESPN’s Nick Wagoner . After the game, Jennifer Lee Chan of NBC Sports Bay Area reported that Evans didn’t tear his Achilles, “but he will miss a little time.” The Niners face the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7 before going on bye in Week 8, so fantasy managers should plan not to have Evans for at least the next two weeks, if not longer. Rams WR Davante Adams (hamstring) Losing to the previously 1-4 Cardinals would have been bad enough for the Rams in Week 6. But on Monday, head coach Sean McVay told reporters that veteran wide receiver Davante Adams suffered a hamstring injury late in the game that is expected to sideline him for six to 10 weeks. A source told ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler that Adams “hopes to return on the front end of the six- to 10-week time frame, as close to the post-Week 11 bye as possible.” Either way, managers now need to plan not to have Adams for most (if not all) of the rest of the fantasy football regular season. In Adams’ absence, fellow wideout Puka Nacua will continue to be peppered with targets. The Rams could lean more heavily on tight end Tyler Higbee and running back Kyren Williams in the passing game, too. But Adams’ injury is a major blow to the Rams, who are now sitting at 2-4 after entering the season as the Super Bowl favorites. Commanders WR Terry McLaurin (knee) Mike Evans wasn’t the only star receiver who couldn’t finish Monday night’s game. Commanders wide receiver Terry McLaurin was carted off the field with a knee injury late in the first quarter and was ruled out shortly thereafter. Much like with Evans, we might not get updates on McLaurin’s status moving forward until the Commanders can do more testing on Tuesday. But considering the nature of his injury, fantasy managers should already start making contingency plans. Tight end Chig Okonkwo led the Commanders with seven catches for 69 yards in McLaurin’s absence, while Treylon Burks had four catches for 66 yards before getting shaken up late. Stefon Diggs (six catches for 44 yards and a touchdown) already shouldn’t be on waiver wires, but Antonio Williams (three catches for 50 yards) would be worth a pickup if McLaurin’s injury proves to be serious.

item.title: ‘Talk now’ – WNBA fans slam Angel Reese’s critics after she makes Finals history
item.description: Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Angel Reese bounced back in spectacular fashion during Game 2 of the WNBA Finals, and her fans are out on social media questioning her critics. After Game 1 of the WNBA Finals which the Atlanta Dream lost, a lot of fans were questioning Angel Reese. The 24-year-old found herself shut down in the second half of that loss, with the Golden State Valkyries earning many plaudits for their defence. Well, she showed what makes her a superstar in Game 2. Reese responded in style during the Dream’s 79-65 victory even as her team tied up the series. The LSU alum is no stranger to winning a championship, but now it seems she’s coming for the Finals MVP too. Angel Reese becomes youngest player in WNBA history with a 30-point, 15-rebound game Reese ended the game with 30 points and 16 rebounds. She also had two blocks, including one that came accompanied with some iconic trash talk. Doing this in just her first-ever playoff run and her first-ever WNBA Finals is extremely awe-inspiring. In the process, Reese also set some records. She became just the third player in WNBA Finals history to record at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a game. Additionally, she became the youngest player in overall playoff history to reach this landmark as well. Her fans were out in force after this display. “Setting records in the WNBA Finals before Caitlin even makes it past the first round…” one fan commented. “Honestly 30 and 16 in a finals game is just disrespectful and I love that for her,” said another fan. “All of you who were talking smack after Game 1, TALK NOW!” a third comment read. “She’s basically sealed FMVP if the Dream can somehow win this series now,” a fourth fan observed. “Imposed her will. A certain stan club about to be REAL QUIET. The Dream should be up 2-0 right now,” a fifth fan claimed. “What are they gonna say now?” asked a sixth fan. Reese’s performance deserves all the love and then some. The greatest players are defined by how they respond to adversity. She showed in Game 2 that her way of dealing with criticism is by going out and setting records in the next game. Angel has the chance to do something truly historic this year. Read more: Jason Kelce loves how a Kansas City Chiefs fan copied Caitlin Clark’s popular ability ‘This is lame’ – Ex-NCAAF player bashes Enes Kanter over 2026 WNBA Finals announcement ‘Power couple’ – Fans react to Caitlin Clark and Taylor Swift watching Chiefs game together

item.title: Mike Evans injury: 49ers WR to miss some time with injured but not torn Achilles
item.description: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers warms up prior to the game against the Washington Commanders at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Post-game update : Following the 49ers 23-17 win over the Commanders, Jennifer Lee Chan reported she is hearing that Mike Evans will miss “a little time” due to his Achilles injury. Early indications are the tendon is intact, but he likely won’t return until after the bye. Third quarter update : The 49ers offense made their first appearance of the second half and Mike Evans appears to still be in the locker room. The team downgraded him to out, so he will not be returning in this game. Brandin Cooks and Jordan Watkins become the top two wide receivers, while George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey will feature prominently in the passing game the rest of the game. Halftime update : The 49ers announced that Mike Evans is questionable to return with an Achilles injury. San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans suffered a leg injury and walked to the locker room ahead of halftime with a member of the medical staff. Evans caught a 16-yard pass from Brock Purdy and went to the ground with it. He seemed to be in some pain and medical staff came out. A replay showed Evans trying to stretch his legs, specifically his right one, before walking off the field and to the locker room. Mike Evans headed to the locker room after this catch 🙏🏼 pic.twitter.com/JzFtUkhXfP — OurSF49ers (@OurSf49ers) October 20, 2026 The risk with signing an old wide receiver in Mike Evans, who had injury issues in the last few years. The risk the Niners took, as he walks off with another injury. 🎥 @sluggahjells pic.twitter.com/vkp1FLOz4P — The Whole Delivery (@TWDTV1) October 20, 2026 That doesn’t look good. Mike Evans walks to lockeroom after hurting his lower leg. Let’s wait for the report. @49ers #MikeEvans pic.twitter.com/igVRwkfWjd — vernkpix (@vernKPIX) October 20, 2026 Evans has been on the injury report with rib issues, but had an Achilles injury added to start this week. It appears he aggravated something in his right leg.

item.title: How Ben Simmons' Achilles injury derailed his NBA comeback and intriguing documentary
item.description: One of the biggest moves the Sacramento Kings made during the offseason was taking a chance on former All-Star Ben Simmons , who missed all of the 2025-26 season to focus on rehabilitation recovering from lingering injuries in his back and knees. His resurgence was profiled by ESPN in their E60 series "Being Ben ," a 60-minute in-depth documentary that goes behind the scenes into Simmons' thoughts and emotions upon his return to the NBA and overcoming past wounds. The documentary, hosted by ESPN's Andscape senior writer Marc Spears, premiered on ESPN on Sunday, Oct. 18 at 4 p.m. ET. The a non-fiction motion picture took a peak into Simmons' life away from the NBA, how he's processed his career up to this point and what he has been up to during his time away. Simmons was a free agent before choosing to commit to Sacramento, and there was tremendous interest in his comeback story. However, all the excitement for the documentary's release was derailed just hours later when the Kings announced Simmons tore his right Achilles' tendon during a live practice drill – likely ending his season before it even began. Spears told USA TODAY in a phone interview that he spoke to Simmons a day before the documentary aired and that he was excited for the film. Spears said the injury occurred "likely, probably within the hour" before the documentary debuted. "It's sad because after people watched it, I think it sets in and the resonation with it was extremely strong and people are feeling it and digging it." Spears said. "And then all of a sudden you just get this gut punch after you just watch this documentary of what just happened to Ben." The Kings will continue to honor his contract; so Simmons' $3.5 million is still guaranteed, which means he won't have to go through rehabilitation alone. He'll have the support of the Kings organization. Members of the organization voice support The Kings are certainly distressed about Simmons' injury but have pledged their support in his rehab journey. Kings rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr. told reporters that losing Simmons is "bad news" and "changes a lot" but provided words of encouragement and suppport him. "We're all here for him. We his brothers," Acuff said. "We just want to continue this journey for him. He got us with him through everything. He has a family in us. Just really praying for him and hope everything goes well." Kings head coach Doug Christie was about to make Simmons a captain. He worked his way into the starting lineup during the preseason after he was initially projected as the backup point guard to Acuff. Christie called the injury a "gut punch" to the team. "We all love Ben and (we're) going to support Ben," Christie said. "A part of it is this is sports and that's where we have to come in here and be the breath underneath their wings to lift them. item.content:encoded: One of the biggest moves the Sacramento Kings made during the offseason was taking a chance on former All-Star Ben Simmons , who missed all of the 2025-26 season to focus on rehabilitation recovering from lingering injuries in his back and knees. His resurgence was profiled by ESPN in their E60 series "Being Ben ," a 60-minute in-depth documentary that goes behind the scenes into Simmons' thoughts and emotions upon his return to the NBA and overcoming past wounds. The documentary, hosted by ESPN's Andscape senior writer Marc Spears, premiered on ESPN on Sunday, Oct. 18 at 4 p.m. ET. The a non-fiction motion picture took a peak into Simmons' life away from the NBA, how he's processed his career up to this point and what he has been up to during his time away. Simmons was a free agent before choosing to commit to Sacramento, and there was tremendous interest in his comeback story. However, all the excitement for the documentary's release was derailed just hours later when the Kings announced Simmons tore his right Achilles' tendon during a live practice drill – likely ending his season before it even began. Spears told USA TODAY in a phone interview that he spoke to Simmons a day before the documentary aired and that he was excited for the film. Spears said the injury occurred "likely, probably within the hour" before the documentary debuted. "It's sad because after people watched it, I think it sets in and the resonation with it was extremely strong and people are feeling it and digging it." Spears said. "And then all of a sudden you just get this gut punch after you just watch this documentary of what just happened to Ben." The Kings will continue to honor his contract; so Simmons' $3.5 million is still guaranteed, which means he won't have to go through rehabilitation alone. He'll have the support of the Kings organization. Members of the organization voice support The Kings are certainly distressed about Simmons' injury but have pledged their support in his rehab journey. Kings rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr. told reporters that losing Simmons is "bad news" and "changes a lot" but provided words of encouragement and suppport him. "We're all here for him. We his brothers," Acuff said. "We just want to continue this journey for him. He got us with him through everything. He has a family in us. Just really praying for him and hope everything goes well." Kings head coach Doug Christie was about to make Simmons a captain. He worked his way into the starting lineup during the preseason after he was initially projected as the backup point guard to Acuff. Christie called the injury a "gut punch" to the team. "We all love Ben and (we're) going to support Ben," Christie said. "A part of it is this is sports and that's where we have to come in here and be the breath underneath their wings to lift them. We'll be there for him. He'll be there for us as we work our way through it." Guard Malik Monk summed up it the best, saying the team was obviously upset about the news. "It definitely wasn't supposed to happen that way with all the work that he put in just to come back," Monk told reporters Monday, Oct. 19. "For him to not even make it to the regular-season, we're just bummed out for him. I feel like everybody is." The Kings have had their injury list grow rapidly before they even could play a regular-season game. Monk has an ankle injury he's slowly coming back from. Maxime Raynaud is recovering from a knee injury he suffered in a preseason game against the Golden State Warriors. Dylan Cardwell had to get a tooth replacement early in training camp. "The Kings right now, it's one thing that have some injuries through the course of the season, but all these injuries before you even play one game is certainly debilitating to the team, no pun intended," Spears said. Simmons' doc still offers pleny of intrigue Simmons' injury could not have come at a worst time. He was just getting into basketball form. Christie was looking at making him a starter, naming him a captain and it appeared the Simmons comeback was alive and well. Now that comeback is delayed for presumably another year. "He felt like he got his super cape back," Spears said. "He was mentally healthy, physically healthy. And I also think he was much stronger than he's ever been. People, I think, forget that, he's all of 6-foot-10 and I think he probably put on about 20 pounds of muscle at least from the last time he played. So, it was great to see him with his physical and mentals back, like see what he could potentially be." Spears believed that Simmons was as good as, if not, better than anybody on the Kings during the limited stints he had during preseason. There was "certainly a reason to be excited about him and what he was doing," Spears said. "I think the city of Sacramento and their fans weren't the only ones that seemed like they we're rooting for him," Spears told USA TODAY. "It seemed like NBA fans all over the world were rooting for him. I mean, he's still going to have his haters. You know, that that doesn't change, but I think he had a lot more love than he did hate and a lot of people were rooting for him." Simmons was entering his eighth NBA season and his first season with the Kings. He has career averages of 15.8 points, 8.1 rebounds, 8.2 assists, 1.7 steals and 0.9 blocks per game. Although his preseason numbers were a shell of that, it was the potential to get back to his previous form that provided excitement in California's capital. Still, despite Simmons season coming to an abrupt end, Spears says there's still power in the ESPN film documenting Simmons' trials and tribulations. "I really hope that Ben's injury doesn't dissuade anybody from watching this E60," Spears said. "I'm really really proud of it. I think it's extremely great and people will learn a lot about him. He's pretty unapologetic and not really trying to like sway how everybody may feel about him. I think he's just being himself. I think what's next for Ben is, it's just not over. "There is a next for Ben. He's only 30," Spears added. "I think it's important to like check out this documentary to learn more about him and who knows, maybe we decide to add a chapter, to the next chapter of Ben Simmons. He's gonna stay in Sacramento and rehab with the support of the franchise. So, again, he's not doing alone. Um, But I think it just makes his story, this latest pitfall for him even more intriguing because before the injury, just looked like the guy that you saw in Philly, but what more confidence with his shot. I'll be really excited to see where he comes from here." This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: How Ben Simmons' Achilles injury derailed his NBA comeback and intriguing documentary

item.title: Conservative media keeps whining about Valkyries, WNBA teams skipping anthem
item.description: Singer Alanis Morissette sings the national anthem before Game Two of the WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries on October 19, 2026 at Chase Center in San Francisco, CA (Icon Sportswire/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) While everyone inside Chase Center for Game 2 of the WNBA Finals had their eyes on Alanis Morissette as she delivered her rendition of the national anthem ahead of tip-off, right-wing media had their eyes on who wasn't: the Valkyries and the Dream. Since 2020, during the height of protests against police brutality and racial inequity that arose after the murder of George Floyd, WNBA players have elected to leave on the court during the playing of the national anthem. Once the song finishes up, players then run onto the court. This continued on Monday, with both the Dream and Valkyries players leaving the court for Morissette's performance, and returning shortly afterwards. Yet despite this being a constant part of WNBA games now for six years, right-wing media outlets continue to sound the alarm about these players' purportedly un-American activities. After the Valkyries' Game 1 68-64 victory against the Dream, the New York Post published a column attributed to the Post Editorial Board headline "Grow up, WNBA - enough with the National Anthem boycott." It accused the league and its fans of treating viewers like "political hostages" and of "obsessive wokery." It's of course worth reiterating that this is all over something the players didn't do. Outkick - a right-wing sports blog the WNBA credentialed to cover the finals - also posted a video of the teams leaving the court for Game 2 with the caption, "Same league. Same disrespect. The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries skip the anthem AGAIN before Game 2 of the WNBA Finals, then stroll back out when it's over," ending the post with an American flag emoji, which riled up the outlet's followers in the replies. Outkick's Dan Zaksheske also highlighted this action in Game 1 with a caption that seemed to indicate he was unaware that this has been ongoing for years. "Both the Dream and the Valkyries left the court prior to the playing of the National Anthem before Game 1 of the WNBA Finals," he wrote . "Both teams also returned to the floor seconds after the anthem concluded. They literally left the floor for only the two minutes the anthem was played. Guess that's just part of the pregame routine though." For what it's worth, there is a rule that requires team members "to stand and line up in a dignified posture along the sidelines or on the foul line during the playing of the National Anthem." However, as The Spun's Andrew Holleran noted in a story published Monday , this could be only a requirement if a player, coach or staffer is on the court during the anthem, which neither side was. Game 3 will take place in Atlanta on Wednesday, when this topic will almost certainly come up again from the same people. More Valkyries - Ballhalla is booming, and

item.title: Bears Announce Concerning Kyle Monangai Injury News Before Patriots Game
item.description: Bears running back Kyle Monangai faces an uncertain return from turf toe ahead of Thursday's Patriots game after missing two straight weeks. Getty The Bears welcomed quarterback and 2024 No. 1 overall draft pick Caleb Williams back from injury on Sunday as Chicago bounced back from a one-sided loss to Green Bay Packers in Week 5 to cruise past the Atlanta Falcons, 31-23. Williams completed 30 of 36 pass attempts for 305 yards and a touchdown for the Bears, but the team managed just 98 rushing yards in total in the absence of second-year running back Kyle Monangai who has already rushed for at least 100 yards in two of his four games before missing both the Packers and Falcons games with a combination of injuries. On Monday, just three days before the Bears’ Thursday Night Football clash with the New England Patriots, Chicago made an announcement with the latest news on Monangai’s status. The Bears announced that Monangai did not practice Monday, leaving his availability in question for Thursday night’s game, according to ESPN reporter Courtney Cronin. Monangai has already missed two games with turf toe, and a third absence would thin Chicago’s backfield on a short week against a fellow 4-2 team. The Bears held only a walk-through, so the team’s estimated injury report projected participation. Linebackers T.J. Edwards and Jack Sanborn and guard Jonah Jackson also sat out, according to Bears reporter Kevin Fishbain . Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson and linebacker Keyshaun Elliott were listed as full participants. The son of Cameroonian immigrants, Monangai starred at Don Bosco Prep in New Jersey, where recruiters favored a bigger teammate over the 5-foot-9, 200-pound back. “They all saw me, but nobody took a chance on me,” Monangai said, according to CBS Sports . item.content:encoded: Bears running back Kyle Monangai faces an uncertain return from turf toe ahead of Thursday's Patriots game after missing two straight weeks. Getty The Bears welcomed quarterback and 2024 No. 1 overall draft pick Caleb Williams back from injury on Sunday as Chicago bounced back from a one-sided loss to Green Bay Packers in Week 5 to cruise past the Atlanta Falcons, 31-23. Williams completed 30 of 36 pass attempts for 305 yards and a touchdown for the Bears, but the team managed just 98 rushing yards in total in the absence of second-year running back Kyle Monangai who has already rushed for at least 100 yards in two of his four games before missing both the Packers and Falcons games with a combination of injuries. On Monday, just three days before the Bears’ Thursday Night Football clash with the New England Patriots, Chicago made an announcement with the latest news on Monangai’s status. The Bears announced that Monangai did not practice Monday, leaving his availability in question for Thursday night’s game, according to ESPN reporter Courtney Cronin. Monangai has already missed two games with turf toe, and a third absence would thin Chicago’s backfield on a short week against a fellow 4-2 team. The Bears held only a walk-through, so the team’s estimated injury report projected participation. Linebackers T.J. Edwards and Jack Sanborn and guard Jonah Jackson also sat out, according to Bears reporter Kevin Fishbain . Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson and linebacker Keyshaun Elliott were listed as full participants. The son of Cameroonian immigrants, Monangai starred at Don Bosco Prep in New Jersey, where recruiters favored a bigger teammate over the 5-foot-9, 200-pound back. “They all saw me, but nobody took a chance on me,” Monangai said, according to CBS Sports . Rutgers coach Greg Schiano did, and Monangai finished with 3,221 rushing yards , second most in program history, after leading the Big Ten with 1,262 yards in 2023. The Bears drafted him in the seventh round, No. 233 overall, in 2025, and he ran for 783 yards and five touchdowns as a rookie, including a 176-yard game at Cincinnati, according to the team’s website. Now in his second NFL season, he is listed at 5-foot-8 and 207 pounds. Kyle Monangai’s Injury Timeline Monangai last played in Week 4, rushing for 146 yards and two touchdowns on 30 carries against the New York Jets . Through those four games, he totaled 60 carries for 324 yards and three scores, a 5.4-yard average, and added five receptions for 39 yards, according to the team’s website. Turf toe and a lesser thumb issue then kept him out of the Week 5 loss to the Green Bay Packers and the Week 6 win over the Atlanta Falcons. Head coach Ben Johnson called the injury week-to-week. “As far as I know, he’s trending in the right direction,” Johnson said, according to the Chicago Sun-Times . Monangai has not practiced in two weeks, and a Week 8 return at the Seattle Seahawks is the more realistic target, according to Sports Illustrated , since Chicago plays on a short week. The Bears then rest 11 days before the Nov. 2 game at Seattle. Read More From Heavy What Bears’ Case Keenum Decision Means for Caleb Williams vs. Falcons Chicago Bears Outlook vs. New England Patriots Without Kyle Monangai Chicago’s ground game declined in his absence after ranking first in the league through the opening month. The Bears ran for 81 yards on 24 carries against Green Bay and 98 yards on 33 carries against Atlanta. D’Andre Swift leads the backfield with Roschon Johnson in a complementary role. Quarterback Williams returned from a three-game absence with a hamstring injury as Chicago scored 31 points against Atlanta, according to Sports Illustrated . Though both teams are 4-2, the Patriots are the hotter one coming into Thursday, winning three in a row. But they lost three starting offensive linemen in Week 6, and oddsmakers list Chicago as a 2.5-point home favorite. Kickoff is set for 8:15 p.m. ET at Soldier Field, and Tuesday and Wednesday practice reports will show whether Monangai takes part. item.title: Rays And Brewers Face Off In World Series That Undermines MLB’s Salary Cap Push
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays won the ALCS over the Cleveland Guardians in six games and will now face the Milwaukee Brewers who swept the Dodgers. (Photo by Mike Carlson/MLB Photos via Getty Images) MLB Photos via Getty Images It wasn’t supposed to be like this. For months, Major League Baseball has pushed – in ads on its MLB Network channel and on MLB.com – that economic disparity was making it impossible for low-payroll clubs in small media markets to compete. The Dodgers were well on their way to their third straight World Series championship and would become not only the first three-time champion since the 1998-2000 Yankees, but also the first National League team to pull off the threepeat. Then, the baseball gods got involved. The 2026 World Series will see the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays face off, with one being crowned champion for the very first time. Of the four teams that made the League Championship Series, there was the Dodgers – the Goliath of the league, with the #1 ranked Competitive Balance Tax (CBT), or more commonly called the Luxury Tax payroll projected by FanGraphs to be $422 million – facing off against the #19 ranked Brewers at $154 million. All the Brewers did was sweep the Dodgers, who looked every bit the part of the league’s oldest team in the league. On the American League side, the #28 ranked Tampa Bay Rays ($110 million CBT payroll) faced off against the #29 Cleveland Guardians with a skinny $103 million CBT payroll. Only the Miami Marlins, with an $86 million Luxury Tax payroll, came in lower. The ALCS wasn’t as lopsided as the NLCS, but it highlighted everything about how this year is simply different in so many ways. Pitching from both teams was sharp, sans Game 6, where it wasn’t until 4.2 innings pitched that the Guardians had their first strikeout of the game (Espino struck out Mesa, Jr.). And while it got dicey in the top of the 8th, ultimately the Rays prevailed 7-3 when Yandy Diaz crushed a 2-RBI home run to right to ultimately give the Rays the 4-2 series win and punch their ticket to the Fall Classic . The Brewers, in MLB’s smallest media market, will face the Tampa Bay Rays in what might be best described as the peak-analytics World Series ever played. None of this will alter the league’s trajectory of pushing for a salary cap and locking the players out come December 1st. It’s an anomaly, which they will point to, reminding everyone that the last time a small payroll team won before 2026 was the Kansas City Royals in 2015. But there have been changes since then, namely the number of teams in the playoffs and how teams are seeded. In other words, the playoffs are random enough that players will say 2026 is another reason to fight against a salary cap. The MLB Players Association has stayed quiet through it all. item.content:encoded: The Tampa Bay Rays won the ALCS over the Cleveland Guardians in six games and will now face the Milwaukee Brewers who swept the Dodgers. (Photo by Mike Carlson/MLB Photos via Getty Images) MLB Photos via Getty Images It wasn’t supposed to be like this. For months, Major League Baseball has pushed – in ads on its MLB Network channel and on MLB.com – that economic disparity was making it impossible for low-payroll clubs in small media markets to compete. The Dodgers were well on their way to their third straight World Series championship and would become not only the first three-time champion since the 1998-2000 Yankees, but also the first National League team to pull off the threepeat. Then, the baseball gods got involved. The 2026 World Series will see the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays face off, with one being crowned champion for the very first time. Of the four teams that made the League Championship Series, there was the Dodgers – the Goliath of the league, with the #1 ranked Competitive Balance Tax (CBT), or more commonly called the Luxury Tax payroll projected by FanGraphs to be $422 million – facing off against the #19 ranked Brewers at $154 million. All the Brewers did was sweep the Dodgers, who looked every bit the part of the league’s oldest team in the league. On the American League side, the #28 ranked Tampa Bay Rays ($110 million CBT payroll) faced off against the #29 Cleveland Guardians with a skinny $103 million CBT payroll. Only the Miami Marlins, with an $86 million Luxury Tax payroll, came in lower. The ALCS wasn’t as lopsided as the NLCS, but it highlighted everything about how this year is simply different in so many ways. Pitching from both teams was sharp, sans Game 6, where it wasn’t until 4.2 innings pitched that the Guardians had their first strikeout of the game (Espino struck out Mesa, Jr.). And while it got dicey in the top of the 8th, ultimately the Rays prevailed 7-3 when Yandy Diaz crushed a 2-RBI home run to right to ultimately give the Rays the 4-2 series win and punch their ticket to the Fall Classic . The Brewers, in MLB’s smallest media market, will face the Tampa Bay Rays in what might be best described as the peak-analytics World Series ever played. None of this will alter the league’s trajectory of pushing for a salary cap and locking the players out come December 1st. It’s an anomaly, which they will point to, reminding everyone that the last time a small payroll team won before 2026 was the Kansas City Royals in 2015. But there have been changes since then, namely the number of teams in the playoffs and how teams are seeded. In other words, the playoffs are random enough that players will say 2026 is another reason to fight against a salary cap. The MLB Players Association has stayed quiet through it all. Reached for comment after the Brewers won the NLCS and advanced to the World Series, MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer said, “I’m gonna let the moment speak for itself.” There will be questions as to how relevant the two teams will be nationally after the Dodgers, with all their star power, were shoved out the door. There’s still the underdog story. The Rays will play in the World Series for the third time, after last losing to the Dodgers in six games in the pandemic-shortened 60-game regular season of 2020. For the Brewers, it will be their first appearance since 1982. So, competitive parity, at least for this year, is a thing. Baseball fans will be treated to a first-time World Series Champion. After that… get ready for a long, cold winter as, regardless of the optics with these two teams facing off for baseball’s ultimate crown, the owners will go to the mat for a salary cap system, a lockout, and possibly lost regular-season games in 2027. The World Series on FOX starts on Friday, Oct 23rd at 8pm ET. This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.title: 10 things to know about the Tampa Bay Rays, Brewers' World Series foe
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers now know that it'll be the Tampa Bay Rays that they face in the 2026 World Series. Somebody will be walking away with the first championship in franchise history, dropping the number of MLB franchises without a World Series title from five to four (sorry, Seattle Mariners, Colorado Rockies and San Diego Padres). Here's what to know about the Rays: How did the Brewers do against the Rays this year? The Brewers beat the Rays in two out of three games at American Family Field, but you have to go all the way back to the first week of the season. March 30: Rays 3, Brewers 2 : After Milwaukee started the year 3-0, it suffered its first defeat at the hands of the Rays in a tight game when Nick Fortes hit a two-out RBI double in the ninth against Trevor Megill. William Contreras hit a two-run homer for Milwaukee. Kyle Harrison recorded eight strikeouts over five innings in his Milwaukee debut. March 31: Brewers 6, Rays 2: Brandon Woodruff's season debut went well despite a pair of solo homers allowed. Brice Turang hit a three-run homer against Rays ace Shane McClanahan (now injured and out for the year) to give his team a 3-2 lead in the fifth. Gary Sánchez and Jake Bauers later added homers. Miz allowed a two-run homer to Yandy Díaz in the third but Turang answered with a two-run homer in the bottom half. The game turned on a six-run eighth, where Christian Yelich, Garrett Mitchell, Blake Perkins and David Hamilton all drove in runs. The "market size" concept isn't entirely easy to define. The Brewers were ranked 19th in MLB in total payroll allocations by the end of 2026, and Tampa Bay was 28th out of 30, and Milwaukee is often regarded as the smallest market in MLB. Somebody will be walking away with the first championship in franchise history, dropping the number of MLB franchises without a World Series title from five to four (sorry, Seattle Mariners, Colorado Rockies and San Diego Padres). Here's what to know about the Rays: How did the Brewers do against the Rays this year? The Brewers beat the Rays in two out of three games at American Family Field, but you have to go all the way back to the first week of the season. March 30: Rays 3, Brewers 2 : After Milwaukee started the year 3-0, it suffered its first defeat at the hands of the Rays in a tight game when Nick Fortes hit a two-out RBI double in the ninth against Trevor Megill. William Contreras hit a two-run homer for Milwaukee. Kyle Harrison recorded eight strikeouts over five innings in his Milwaukee debut. March 31: Brewers 6, Rays 2: Brandon Woodruff's season debut went well despite a pair of solo homers allowed. Brice Turang hit a three-run homer against Rays ace Shane McClanahan (now injured and out for the year) to give his team a 3-2 lead in the fifth. Gary Sánchez and Jake Bauers later added homers. April 1: Brewers 8, Rays 2. Jacob Misiorowski outdueled Drew Rasmussen in a battle that we couldn't have known would be the likely Game 1 matchup in the World Series. Miz allowed a two-run homer to Yandy Díaz in the third but Turang answered with a two-run homer in the bottom half. The game turned on a six-run eighth, where Christian Yelich, Garrett Mitchell, Blake Perkins and David Hamilton all drove in runs. An incredible irony: During labor debate over salary cap, two of baseball's smallest markets meet With the threat of a lockout looming after the season, centered around the owners' perspective that competitive imbalance in Major League Baseball calls for a salary cap, it's incredibly ironic that two of the smallest markets are competing for a World Series. The "market size" concept isn't entirely easy to define. The Brewers were ranked 19th in MLB in total payroll allocations by the end of 2026, and Tampa Bay was 28th out of 30, and Milwaukee is often regarded as the smallest market in MLB. Any way you slice it, the World Series will be the first since 2015 (Kansas City vs. San Francisco) to feature two cities outside the nation's 10 biggest. The team's top two pitchers are former Brewers The Rays have gotten big-time contributions from top pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, both of whom are former Brewers. Peralta is the obvious one, the 2025 ace of the Brewers traded in the offseason to the New York Mets for Brandon Sproat and Jett Williams. It was a disastrous deal for the Mets even though the two players Milwaukee got back had rough years, with Peralta posting a 4.99 ERA before he was traded to the Rays at the deadline. With Tampa Bay, Peralta has been on a tear. He's allowed two earned runs in 16⅔ playoff innings, and that's on the heels of posting a 0.79 ERA in his final six outings (three earned runs, 34 innings). The Rays have won all nine of his last nine games. Then there's Rasmussen, an all-star this season for the second time who was dealt by the Brewers to the Rays in 2021 for Willy Adames. Though that trade yielded Milwaukee's starting shortstop for the next three-plus years, it has some of the same vibes as the CC Sabathia deal: Milwaukee got what it wanted but paid for it. Rasmussen, a sixth-round pick in 2018, has a career 2.83 ERA and a 1.024 WHIP, and he led AL qualified pitchers with a 0.913 WHIP this season. He went 16-5 this season with 174 strikeouts in 172 innings. Rasmussen pitched in 27 games for Milwaukee in 2020 and 2021. Peralta, of course, is one of the organization's best-ever pitchers, appearing in 211 games (70-42, 3.59 ERA) over the course of eight seasons. One other Brewers-adjacent note: star third baseman Junior Caminero was famously traded by Cleveland (the team Tampa Bay beat in the ALCS) for eventual Brewers pitcher Tobias Myers. Myers was also part of the deal when Milwaukee sent Peralta to the Mets. Brewers general manager Matt Arnold has Rays history When David Stearns took over as Brewers general manager, he hired Matt Arnold away from the Rays to be his No. 2. Arnold, who eventually took over as GM and president of baseball operations, spent nine seasons with the Rays, working alongside general manager Andrew Friedman (now the architect of the Dodgers – the team Arnold's Brewers just beat) and current Rays president of baseball operations Erik Neander. Arnold has helped instill some of the basic tenets in Milwaukee that the Rays have employed, namely the approach that has allowed a small-market team to thrive despite no salary cap in Major League Baseball. The Rays have endured World Series heartbreak before Though the Rays have only been a franchise since 1998, they do have two World Series appearances in 2008 and 2020, coincidentally losing both times to the team that defeated the Brewers earlier in those postseasons. In 2008, the Phillies (who toppled Milwaukee in the National League Division Series) defeated the Rays in five games. In 2020, the Dodgers (who topped Milwaukee in the strange first-round format of the COVID-19 season) topped the Rays in six. In that series, former Brewers outfielder Brett Phillips had a walk-off single that scored the tying run and then the winning run following Dodgers' defensive miscues. The Rays are 3-0 in AL Championship Series. They've made it to the playoffs 10 times since 2008, the same number of times as the Brewers in that stretch. Tampa Bay didn't have a winning season (or even more than 70 wins in a season) for the first 10 years of its existence. Chandler Simpson is probably the fastest human in baseball David Hamilton and Garrett Mitchell are two of the fastest four players getting from home plate to first base in Major League Baseball, at least according to Statcast metrics. But nobody is faster than Rays outfielder Chandler Simpson. Simpson's 3.97-second speed is easily the fastest in baseball (the next is 4.04). He's also an above-average defender in the outfield, but he has the ability to create serious havoc on the basepaths. He went 2-for-3 in Game 5 with a run scored and a stolen base. Junior Caminero is one of baseball's great young stars Third baseman Junior Caminero, at age 23, is easily the top offensive player of the team. The two-time all-star hit 42 home runs this year after hitting 45 last year, played in all 162 games, posted an .885 OPS and won't even be arbitration eligible until 2028. He's one of the best stars in the game, and Baseball Reference regards him as 5.7 wins above replacement, easily the best player on the team (though by comparison, the Brewers have two players in Brice Turang at 7.3 and Jacob Misiorowski at 6.5 who rate higher). Caminero hasn't dominated in the playoffs, but he did hit a two-run homer in the clinching Game 6 of the ALCS. The Rays defense is sensational ... probably? Only the Chicago Cubs had a better "defensive runs saved" metric according to Fielding Bible, with a count of 87 that was well ahead of Boston (67) and Milwaukee (62). The Cubs, at 115, were tops. Shortstop Taylor Walls is regarded as one of the five best defenders in all of baseball by that format, with plus assessments of outfielders Victor Mesa Jr., Simpson, Cedric Mullins and Jonny DeLuca. But then there's Outs Above Average produced by Statcast, and the Rays rank just 15th out of 30 MLB teams in that category, basically average. The Cubs are again the cream of the crop (73 OAA), but the Brewers (20) are just as close to the top as to the middle. Ball off a roof? It's normal here The Brewers, of course, already have a memorable playoff moment involving a ball off the roof. That's normal stuff at Tropicana Field, where two of the four catwalk rings around the stadium's roof are in play and oft

item.title: Dream’s Jordin Canada pulls up from Valkyries logo for bonkers WNBA Finals buzzer-beater
item.description: Mandatory Credit: David Gonzales-Imagn Images Dream’s Jordin Canada pulls up from Valkyries logo for bonkers WNBA Finals buzzer-beater appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Angel Resee and the A tlanta Dream let Game 1 of the WNBA Finals “slip away” as they failed to hold onto their fourth quarter lead. They look determined not to make the same mistake again in Game 2, though, as Jordin Canada showed with her buzzer-beating 3-pointer from the logo. O CANADA!!! Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Jordin Canada with a LOGO three to end the third quarter 🎯 The Dream holds a 14-point lead over the Valkyries heading into the fourth! pic.twitter.com/5stkSr9uzE — ClutchPoints (@ClutchPoints) October 20, 2026 The Dream guard dribbled quickly down the court before pulling up from midcourt to bank in the bucket. That shot gave the Dream a commanding 14-point lead heading into the fourth quarter. Jordin Canada has been one of the Dream’s most consistent performers during this postseason run. She reached double-digits in points in each of her first five playoff games and is one of the team’s top playoff scorers . However, her influence as blunted by the Golden State Valkyries’ defense in Game 1 as she was limited to just eight points in 38 minutes. The return of backcourt mate Allisha Gray from her hand injury provided a timely boost, although Gray was understandably rusty as she shot just 5 of 19. Angel Reese also had a somewhat understated Game 1 by her high standards, finishing with just 14 points and 12 rebounds. But the Dream star was on a mission in Game 2. She surpassed her Game 1 points total by halftime as she racked up 15 points and seven rebounds in an amazing first-half performance . Led by her fine play, the Dream managed to tie up the WNBA Finals at 1-1. Aside from her halfcourt heave, though, Jordin Canada still struggled with her shot as she went just 3 of 13 for 12 points. Atlanta will need Canada to get back to her best for the remainder of the series if they are to overcome the Valkyries in the end. Related: Angel Reese demands Dream fans ‘pull up and pop out’ for WNBA Finals Game 3 vs. Valkyries Related: Angel Reese, Sheryl Swoopes share special moment after Dream’s Game 2 win in WNBA Finals

item.title: Key takeaways from heartbreaking Washington Commanders loss to San Francisco 49ers
item.description: BOX SCORE We all know what happened in Week 5. We don’t have to go over that debacle against the Giants for the 1,000 th time. Washington said all the right things, took accountability for that mess and maintained a unified front while vowing to be better moving forward. Head coach Dan Quinn even turned his hat around. While seemingly silly, it was a symbol that he and the Commanders were ditching the relaxed vibe and taking things more seriously. Proving that they were better and had rebounded well was a tough task, however, considering they had to fly across the country to play the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers on Monday night. The 49ers were more talented at most every spot, even with San Francisco beset by with injuries. Leaving with a win was always considered tough – it would’ve been huge considering the dismal state of the NFC East – but remaining competitive seemed necessary. Despite an awful first half, the Commanders certainly were. And wouldn’t ya know it, this game also came down to a last-second scenario, with the Commanders pushing to win the game with no timeouts and less than a minute left. Could the Commanders handle this late-game scenario? The game management wasn’t the issue here, but the result wasn’t any better. The game was in the balance, with the Commanders pushing hard for a score with less that an minute left. In the decisive play, Daniels was called for an intentional grounding call that generated a loss of down and a 10 second runoff, setting up a presumptive last-second chuck into the end zone. Jayden Daniels’ final pass never left his hand, leaving this comeback attempt just short of a miracle finish. Jayden Daniels gets sacked as time expires. 49ers win 23-17 pic.twitter.com/7NMR0apwfI — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) October 20, 2026 The Commanders lost this one 23-17, a heartbreaker that drops the Commanders to 1-4-1 on the season heading into their bye. Here are some key takeaways from this Week 6 defeat: Dan Quinn’s seat cools a bit The Commanders attempted to convert a fourth down in the first half that went completely wrong. They were flagged for an illegal shift on the play, but quarterback Jayden Daniels threw the ball away over working to complete a pass that would earn a first down. It was a messy play that has become all too common. Then a video clip from the broadcast went viral, where Quinn seemed to look confused about what down it was. This is a very tough look for Dan Quinn. Looks like he thought the 4th down play was 3rd down. Very tough especially after last week pic.twitter.com/KUU8D2S81d — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) October 20, 2026 Whether that was the case or not, it was a bad look after letting the clock run out in overtime against the Giants and within makeable range of a decisive field goal. Back to what we discussed in the intro, Quinn needed a solid performance and signs of hope for better following what happened in Week 5. Netflix/The Ringer reporter Tom Pelissero stated that owner Josh
